promptHtml: Your design passes its testbench, and the board is plugged in by USB. Put in order the steps that put the design on the board.
explanationHtml: The bitstream must exist before anything can be programmed, and the Hardware Manager must find the board's FPGA before it can program it. DONE lights when the FPGA has loaded the whole bitstream, and from then on the chip is your circuit.
steps: Open Target, then Auto Connect: Vivado finds the FPGA on the board.
Program Device, with the bitstream Vivado wrote.
The DONE LED lights, and your design runs.

promptHtml: Every Vivado report starts with a header that names the design and the part it was built for. Below are two lines of the header of hello's Utilization report.
explanationHtml: xc7a100tcsg324-1, the Artix-7 100T in the 324-pin package on the Arty A7-100T. A bitstream fits only the part it was built for: an Arty A7-35T needs a build for its own part, xc7a35ticsg324-1L, as level 1's project said.
ask: Which part was hello built for?

promptHtml: The terminal on your PC will listen at 115,200 baud: 115,200 bits a second. hello passes LAST to its uart_tx, which makes each bit last LAST + 1 cycles of the board's 100 MHz clock. Fill in LAST.
explanationHtml: One bit lasts 100,000,000 ÷ 115,200 = 868 cycles, to the nearest cycle, and the timer counts 0 to LAST, so LAST is 867. A design and a terminal set to different rates still exchange bits, but each side reads them at the wrong moments, and the terminal shows the wrong characters.
before: parameter int               TBITS = 10,      // uart_tx's timer width
after: parameter int               PBITS = 20,      // press's counter width
parameter logic [PBITS-1:0] HOLD  = 999_999  // about 10 ms at 100 MHz

promptHtml: Your board's mode jumper is set so that the FPGA loads the board's flash memory at power-on, and the flash holds a demo design. You program hello, then unplug the board and plug it back in. Put in order what happens.
explanationHtml: Programming over USB writes the FPGA's configuration memory, which keeps the bitstream only while the board has power. At every power-on this board loads its flash memory, so after the second plug-in the demo runs again, not hello. To keep a design, you would write it into the flash, which this course does not need.
steps: You plug in the board, and the FPGA loads the demo from the flash memory.
You program `hello` from the Hardware Manager, and `hello` runs.
You unplug the board, and the FPGA loses its configuration.
You plug it in again, and the FPGA loads the demo from the flash memory again.

promptHtml: Below are two lines of the header of hello's Utilization report, the one written at the end of a build.
explanationHtml: Routed: placed and wired up, the design the bitstream is written from, so this report counts what you program. The course's builds also write utilization_synth.rpt after synthesis, which says Synthesized, and its counts can still change (lesson 6.4).
ask: In what state was the design when Vivado wrote this report?
